title: Post-Caesarean Analgesia (PROSPECT 2026)
sources: Critical Vector — Cesarean Section Analgesia: The 2026 PROSPECT Update

Crowe G, Atterton B, Roofthooft E, et al; PROSPECT Working Group (ESRA). Pain management after elective caesarean section under neuraxial anaesthesia — updated SR and PROSPECT recommendations. Anaesthesia 2026;81:819-839

changelog.change: Initial entry — the 2026 PROSPECT six-domain recommendation for post-caesarean analgesia under neuraxial anaesthesia.

summary: Three load-bearing pillars: (1) a single neuraxial long-acting opioid, (2) scheduled — not as-needed — paracetamol + NSAID, (3) a single IV dexamethasone dose after delivery. Everything else is an addition. Oral opioids are the rescue backstop, not a routine component.

body.text: Six-domain recommendation (elective caesarean under neuraxial anaesthesia)

rows: Intrathecal morphine 50–100 mcg OR diamorphine up to 300 mcg. Epidural alternative 2–3 mg morphine if a catheter is in place. A single preoperative dose gives many hours of analgesia without the systemic opioid burden.

If intrathecal morphine was NOT used: wound infiltration or a fascial plane block (TAP, transversalis fascia, QL, ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric) intraoperatively after delivery. None is superior to the others — the abdominal wall just needs covering by one mechanism.
Scheduled paracetamol AND NSAIDs, started peri- or intraoperatively, continued postoperatively — not rescue dosing. Two non-opioid mechanisms established before the neuraxial opioid wears off.
Single dose 8–10 mg IV after delivery — independent analgesic contribution plus antiemetic benefit in a high-PONV population.
Joel-Cohen incision (not Pfannenstiel), non-closure of the peritoneum, abdominal binder — incision and closure choices measurably change the pain trajectory before any drug.
TENS as an adjunct. Oral opioids reserved for breakthrough pain or when the preferred regional techniques can't be used — the backstop, not a fourth pillar.

body.text: Operating principles: default to intrathecal morphine/diamorphine whenever neuraxial anaesthesia is the primary technique; schedule paracetamol + NSAID from the start (don't wait for the patient to ask); give the single dexamethasone dose after delivery; if intrathecal morphine isn't in the plan, default to a fascial plane block or wound infiltration rather than leaning harder on systemic opioids; treat surgical technique as part of the analgesic plan.

buildNote: Tier 3, ~6-month review. Elective-caesarean-specific; emergency caesarean under GA and the failed-block scenario are separate.
